section.title: Stand in Awe of God
section.sectionRationale: Amid a book that keeps finding vapor everywhere, the Teacher turns to the one place where solid ground is found: the presence of God. He counsels reverence in worship, restraint in speech, and faithfulness in vows, because God is in heaven and we are on earth. The passage answers the whole book's ache with a single steadying command that will become its conclusion, fear God. It is the still center of Ecclesiastes, where the futility of empty words meets the weight of the living God.
section.thesis: Because God is in heaven and we are on earth, we are to draw near to listen rather than to babble, to keep our words few and our vows faithful, and above all to fear God, the one anchor in a world of vapor.
section.frameNote: Two movements: guard your steps, approaching God to listen with few words rather than the sacrifice of fools; and fulfill your vows, keeping faith with what you promise God, closing on the summons that anchors the book, fear God.

verses.text: Guard your steps when you go to the house of {{elohim|God}}. Draw near to listen rather than to offer the sacrifice of fools, who do not know that they do wrong.
Do not be quick to speak, and do not be hasty in your heart to utter a word before {{elohim|God}}. For God is in heaven and you are on earth. So let your words be few.
As a dream comes through many cares, so the speech of a fool comes with many words.
When you make a vow to God, do not delay in fulfilling it, because He takes no pleasure in fools. Fulfill your vow.
It is better not to vow than to make a vow and not fulfill it.
Do not let your mouth cause your flesh to sin, and do not tell the messenger that your vow was a mistake. Why should God be angry with your words and destroy the work of your hands?
For as many dreams bring {{hevel|futility}}, so do many words. Therefore, fear {{elohim|God}}.

elohim.gloss: God, the Deity. Ecclesiastes always names God as Elohim, the sovereign Creator who is in heaven while we are on earth. In this passage He is the God whose house we enter with guarded steps, before whom our words must be few, and whom we are finally commanded to fear.

hevel.gloss: Vapor, breath, mist. The keyword of the book, rendered futility, meaningless, or fleeting. Here the many words of the fool, like the tangle of many dreams, are hevel, empty breath that vanishes, set against the solid weight of fearing God.

basic.context: After chapters of finding vapor in pleasure, work, wealth, and power, the Teacher turns to worship, the one place where we meet solid ground. He warns us to watch our steps as we come before God: come to listen, not to rattle off the empty religious talk of fools. Because God is in heaven and we are on earth, our words should be few. He then presses the point with vows: if you promise God something, keep it; better to make no vow than to break one. Careless words before God are dangerous. The whole passage lands on one command that becomes the message of the book, fear God. In a world where so much is fleeting, reverence for God is the anchor.
basic.hermeneutics: The key phrase is God is in heaven and you are on earth, which sets the tone: awe, not casualness. The fear of God here is not cringing terror but covenant reverence, the awed, trusting respect owed to the Creator by the creature. The warnings about many words and rash vows are not against prayer or commitment, but against treating God lightly, as if He were an equal to be managed with talk. The passage is the still, positive center that the rest of the book's darkness has been driving toward.
basic.originalLanguages: God is named Elohim, the Creator who is in heaven while we are on earth, and the passage circles from His house, verse 1, to His anger, verse 6, to the command to fear Him, verse 7. Against Him stands hevel, vapor: the many words of the fool are as empty and fleeting as a crowd of dreams. The contrast is the point, empty breath on one side, the weighty reality of God on the other, and the reader is told which to reckon with.
basic.typology: Drawing near to listen rather than to speak points ahead to the greater Word, the Son through whom God has finally spoken, and to whom we are told to listen. The care about vows and truthful speech before God anticipates Christ, who kept perfect faith with the Father and taught let your yes be yes. And the command to fear God is fulfilled in the Son who, in the days of His flesh, was heard because of His reverent submission.
basic.christ: The passage tells us to draw near and listen, and the New Testament says God has spoken finally in His Son, listen to Him. Where our words are vapor and our vows so easily broken, Christ is the faithful and true witness who kept every promise and never sinned with His lips. Through Him we draw near to God with confidence rather than dread, our fear of God deepened into the reverent love of children who have been welcomed home. He is the one whose reverent obedience was fully pleasing to the Father.
basic.god: God is in heaven, exalted and sovereign, not to be handled with careless words or empty ritual. He is holy, so that rash vows and foolish talk before Him are perilous. Yet He is the God who invites us into His house to listen and to draw near, and the fear He commands is the doorway to wisdom and life, not a barrier to it. He takes no pleasure in fools but delights in reverent, faithful worshipers.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 66 says God dwells with the humble and contrite who tremble at His word. Matthew 6 warns against heaping up empty phrases in prayer. James 5 echoes let your yes be yes. Hebrews 12 calls us to worship with reverence and awe, for our God is a consuming fire.
basic.oneStory: In a book that keeps exposing life under the sun as vapor, chapter 5 opens the one door to solid ground: the fear of God. Reverence, restraint, and faithful speech mark the creature who knows that God is in heaven. This is the anchor the whole book has been reaching for, and it finds its fullness in Christ, through whom we draw near to God and learn to fear Him as beloved children.

context.literary:
This short section is a hinge in the book. The long meditation on futility pauses, and for seven verses the Teacher gives what looks like plain instruction for worship. A note on numbering helps: in the Hebrew Bible the first verse of this passage is the last verse of chapter 4, so the Hebrew chapter 5 begins one verse later. The BSB follows the English division.

The passage is built in three pieces, each with its own warning. Verse 1 concerns the act of drawing near: guard your steps, listen rather than sacrifice. Verses 2 and 3 concern prayer: few words, because God is in heaven and you are on earth, and many words are the mark of a fool. Verses 4 to 6 concern vows: do not delay, and better not to vow than to vow and fail. Verse 7 gathers the three into a closing line that sets dreams and words side by side and ends with the command 'fear God.'

The dream image works as a hinge. In verse 3 a dream comes through many cares, and the speech of the fool through many words. In verse 7 the many dreams and the many words both bring futility. That frame, with the dream at both ends, tells the reader that a flood of words in worship is as insubstantial as the images of a restless night.

The movement of the section is from the ground up. It starts with the feet, 'guard your steps,' goes to the heart, 'do not be hasty in your heart,' goes to the mouth, 'do not let your mouth cause your flesh to sin,' and finishes with fear, which governs all three. It is also the first time the book has addressed its reader with a string of imperatives: guard, draw near, do not be quick, fulfill. After chapters of observation, the Teacher finally says what to do.
context.historical:
The 'house of God' is the temple in Jerusalem, and a worshiper going up to it was entering a place of sacrifice and vows. If the book is read against Solomon's reign, the setting is the temple he built, dedicated with a prayer that asks whether God could really dwell on earth when the highest heaven cannot contain Him, 1 Kings 8:27. The reminder in verse 2 that God is in heaven and you are on earth has the same ring, and it keeps the building from turning into a boast.

Sacrifices in Israel were many and varied, and the priests handled them. Some were obligatory, like sin offerings, and some were freewill offerings or the fulfillment of vows, Leviticus 22:21. A vow, a neder, was a voluntary promise made to God, often in a time of need: Jacob at Bethel, Genesis 28:20-22, Hannah for a son, 1 Samuel 1:11, and the psalmist, who promises to enter God's house with offerings, Psalm 66:13-14. Vows were taken seriously. Numbers 30:2 says the one who vows must not break his word, and Deuteronomy 23:21-23 warns that delay becomes sin, while refusing to vow is no sin.

Rash vows were a known danger. Jephthah's vow before battle ended in the sacrifice of his only daughter, Judges 11:30-39. Saul bound his troops by an oath that nearly cost his son's life and left the army starved, 1 Samuel 14:24. Leviticus 5:4-6 even makes provision for the thoughtless oath: someone who swears rashly and later realizes it is guilty and must confess and bring an offering.

The 'messenger' of verse 6 would be the one to whom a worshiper reported a vow. Most likely it was a priest, who in Malachi 2:7 is called the messenger of the LORD of Hosts. To say to him, 'it was a mistake,' was to claim the sort of unintentional error that Leviticus allows for, in order to escape a vow that was no mistake at all.
context.canonical:
The passage draws on the Law and is picked up by the Prophets, Wisdom and Jesus. Its closest source is Deuteronomy 23:21-23, which warns against delay in keeping a vow and says that refusing to vow is not sin. The Teacher's 'better not to vow' is a plain summary of that text. Numbers 30:2 and Psalm 76:11 also say to make and fulfill vows to the LORD.

The warning against the fools' sacrifice joins a prophetic chorus. Samuel told Saul that obedience is better than sacrifice and attentiveness better than the fat of rams, 1 Samuel 15:22. Hosea 6:6 has God say, 'I desire mercy, not sacrifice,' and Micah 6:6-8 answers the question of what to bring with the command to act justly, love mercy and walk humbly. Isaiah 29:13 diagnoses people who draw near with their mouths while their hearts are far away. Proverbs 15:8 and 21:27 call the sacrifice of the wicked detestable.

The counsel on words is echoed throughout Proverbs: 'When words are many, sin is unavoidable,' Proverbs 10:19; even a fool is thought wise if he keeps silent, 17:28; a hasty speaker has less hope than a fool, 29:20; and it is 'a trap' to dedicate something rashly and reconsider the vow afterward, 20:25. Psalm 141:3 turns it into a prayer: 'Set a guard, O LORD, over my mouth.'

Jesus takes up the same subject. He teaches that His followers should not babble like pagans, for the Father knows what they need before they ask, Matthew 6:7-8, and that a plain yes and no should replace oaths, Matthew 5:33-37, a teaching James repeats in James 5:12. He drives the traders out of the temple, John 2:14-17, to restore it as a house of prayer, Matthew 21:12-13. Hebrews recasts the whole approach: we draw near by the blood of Jesus, Hebrews 10:19-22, 'with reverence and awe,' Hebrews 12:28-29.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The Teacher wants his hearers to bring the book's honesty about life into the temple courts. If everything under the sun is a breath, then even worship can be hollowed out, and a lot of religious activity is noise. He writes to people who are busy at the house of God, bringing sacrifices and making vows, and he asks whether they are listening.

His aim is not to discourage worship but to purify it. A person who rushes in with offerings and many words treats God as a business partner to be bargained with or impressed. The Teacher wants them to see that God is not manageable. The ground of the instruction is a simple fact: God is in heaven and you are on earth. From that one fact flow caution, brevity and honest promises.

He also wants them to take their own words seriously. A vow is not a mood. To make one and to treat it lightly is to treat God lightly. He goes so far as to say that it would have been better not to vow at all. The hearers are meant to leave the temple knowing that God is greater than their speech, that He listens to a heart before a gift, and that the right response to such a God is reverent fear.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
This passage is among the most directly prescriptive in the book. It is written in the imperative: guard, draw near, do not be quick, fulfill. The commands apply wherever people come to worship, and the New Testament confirms their substance: reverent listening, restraint in speech and truthfulness in promises, Matthew 5:33-37 and James 1:19.

Some care is needed in applying the details. The instruction about sacrifice and the temple belonged to a setting where the priestly system was in force. Christians do not bring animal sacrifices, and the specific vow system of Israel's law has passed. The principle behind it has not: God desires the listening heart, and He takes promises made in His name seriously.

Nor does 'let your words be few' forbid long prayer. Jesus prayed through the night, Luke 6:12, and Paul tells believers to pray without ceasing, 1 Thessalonians 5:17. The target is hurried, careless and showy speech, not sustained and honest prayer. The passage does not tell believers never to make commitments, but to make them carefully and keep them. A modern example would be marriage vows, membership promises and baptismal commitments, which are to be made with sobriety and kept.

debates.question: Who is 'the messenger' in verse 6?

views.label: A priest or temple official
views.case: A priest is called the messenger of the LORD of Hosts in Malachi 2:7, and vows were reported to the priests. To tell him a vow was a mistake would be to use the language of unintentional sin, Leviticus 5:4-6, to escape a promise. This is the most common view.

views.label: An angel
views.case: The BSB footnote notes that the same word can mean angel. On this reading the vow is overheard by heavenly beings, and calling it a mistake is a denial before God's court.

views.label: A representative sent to collect the vow
views.case: Another suggestion is that the messenger is someone sent by the sanctuary to collect what was promised, so that the excuse is made to a human agent.

debates.bearing: On every reading the person is excusing a deliberate promise as an accident, and the verse says that God is not deceived. Whether the hearer is a priest or an angel, the vow was made before God, and the warning is the same.

debates.question: What is 'the sacrifice of fools' in verse 1?

views.label: Offerings from people who do not listen
views.case: The fools bring sacrifices without attention to what God has said. The comparison with 1 Samuel 15:22 and Hosea 6:6 suggests that the problem is ritual without obedience.

views.label: Offerings from people who sin and think a sacrifice cancels it
views.case: The final clause says they do not know that they do wrong. This points to worshipers who assume that bringing an offering makes up for conduct they never examine, as Proverbs 21:27 warns.

views.label: Sacrifice as such is being devalued
views.case: A few read the verse as a general preference for listening over sacrifice. That goes beyond the text, since the Teacher assumes that sacrifices will be offered and vows paid, and asks only that they come with a listening heart.

debates.bearing: The first two views fit together. Sacrifice offered without listening and without self-examination is the fool's sacrifice. The passage corrects the way the offering is brought, not whether it is brought.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 1 begins with a physical image: shemor raglekha, 'guard your foot.' The Hebrew has a singular 'foot,' and the idiom is about watching how one walks into a sacred place. Exodus 3:5 shows the same instinct: Moses is told to take off his sandals because the ground is holy. The direction that follows, 'draw near to listen,' uses the verb shama, which in Hebrew means both to hear and to obey. The contrast Samuel draws in 1 Samuel 15:22 between obedient hearing and sacrifice is the contrast the Teacher is drawing here.

The 'fools' are the kesilim, the plural of the same word used of the fool in 2:14 and 4:5. They are the stubborn and dull, and the book will return to them throughout. The last clause of verse 1 is compressed in the Hebrew, close to 'for they do not know to do evil.' The BSB reads it as being unaware that they do wrong. The Hebrew can also be taken as an observation that such worshipers do not even know how to tell the difference, and either way the problem is a lack of knowledge, not of enthusiasm.

In verse 2 the phrase 'do not be hasty' translates a verb of hurrying or being agitated, and the thing hurried is the act of bringing out a word, lehotzi davar. A word is something that is brought out of the heart. The heart is the place where it should be held and weighed first. The verse ends with the stark contrast between God ba-shamayim, in heaven, and you al ha-arets, on the earth, which is the language of Psalm 115:16, where the heavens belong to the LORD and the earth He has given to humanity.

Verse 3 uses a word we met in 3:10, 'inyan, occupation or business: a dream comes through the multitude of 'inyan. The restless night is the product of a busy day. The fool's speech is the product of a mind that has been busy with itself.

The key vow vocabulary is neder, a vow, and shalem, to pay or complete, from the root that gives shalom. A vow is something to be made whole, brought to completion. Verse 4's command not to delay, al te'acher leshalmo, repeats almost exactly the Hebrew phrase of Deuteronomy 23:21. Verse 5 echoes the next verse in that passage, where refraining from a vow brings no guilt.

The 'pleasure' of verse 4, chephets, is the word we met in 3:1 for 'purpose.' God takes no chephets in fools, meaning He finds no delight in them. The whole sweep of the book has used chephets for what a person wants or enjoys, and here it describes what God wants.

In verse 6, the 'mistake' is shegagah, the Hebrew word for an unintentional wrong, the category in Leviticus 4 and Numbers 15:22-29. The excuse the worshiper offers is that his vow belongs to that category. The 'messenger' is malak, the word that can mean a human envoy or an angel, as the BSB footnote notes.

Verse 7 is among the hardest verses in the book to render. The Hebrew is compressed and translators supply words to connect dreams, vanity and words. The BSB gives the sense that many dreams and many words are alike futile. The imperative that ends it, 'fear God,' is the book's central command: 3:14 said that God acts so that people fear Him, and 12:13 will end with the same words.

typology.fulfillment: The temple that worshipers entered with care points beyond itself. When Jesus is challenged for clearing it, He speaks of destroying the temple and raising it in three days, and John explains that He meant the temple of His body, John 2:19-21. At His death the temple veil was torn in two, Mark 15:38, and Hebrews says we now enter the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus through the curtain of His body, Hebrews 10:19-22. The care the Teacher asks for is not abolished, since Hebrews adds 'reverence and awe,' 12:28. What changes is that access is given through a person and not a building, and the church itself is built up as a spiritual house, 1 Peter 2:5. The type falls short because the old house could be entered only by a few and only at set times.

The Teacher's preference for listening over the sacrifice of fools has a deeper form in Psalm 40:6-8: 'Sacrifice and offering You did not desire, but my ears You have opened.' Hebrews 10:5-9 hears Christ Himself speaking those words as He comes into the world: 'I have come to do Your will, O God.' The true Worshiper is the one with open ears who obeys perfectly, and His obedience becomes the sacrifice that finally deals with sin. The correspondence is that listening and offering are joined in Him. The Teacher's contrast is therefore not abolished but fulfilled, because the perfect Listener is also the perfect offering.

typology.type: The vow kept and the silent Servant, Ecclesiastes 5:2-6
typology.fulfillment: The Teacher commends few words and fulfilled promises. In Christ both are seen to the full. Before accusers He gave no answer, Matthew 27:12-14, as the Servant who 'did not open His mouth,' Isaiah 53:7, and He entrusted Himself to the One who judges justly, 1 Peter 2:23. His speech is always true, and Paul writes that all the promises of God are 'Yes' in Christ, 2 Corinthians 1:20. The psalm of the suffering righteous says, 'I will fulfill my vows before those who fear You,' Psalm 22:25. The type falls short because the Teacher can only warn people to keep their word, while Christ keeps God's word to humanity and in doing so makes our imperfect keeping of ours bearable.

study.christ:
The passage leads to Christ by the way of access. It begins with a person walking carefully into the house of God, aware that he is a creature before the Creator. The Gospels show what happens to that house when the Son arrives. He calls it His Father's house, drives out the traders in zeal for it, John 2:14-17, and then says that the temple is Himself, John 2:19-21. When He dies the veil is torn from top to bottom, Mark 15:38. The Teacher's instruction to guard your steps is not discarded. It is deepened, because the way in is now a person: 'I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me,' John 14:6. Hebrews tells us to draw near with a sincere heart, in full assurance of faith, Hebrews 10:22, and to approach the throne of grace with confidence, Hebrews 4:16. The confidence is not in our speech but in the Priest who always lives to intercede, Hebrews 7:25.

It leads to Christ by the contrast between a flood of words and a listening ear. The Teacher warns against the sacrifice of fools. Psalm 40:6-8 gives the voice of the true Worshiper, and Hebrews 10:5-9 puts it in the mouth of Christ. He does not rush into God's presence with an offering and a speech. He comes saying, 'I have come to do Your will.' His life is the great act of listening, and His death is the great act of fulfilling.

It leads to Christ by the matter of vows and words. We make promises and break them. The Teacher says it is better not to vow than to vow and not pay. Christ stands as the one who has paid everything the covenant required. Paul says that all the promises of God find their 'Yes' in Him, 2 Corinthians 1:20, and the Savior who gave a plain yes and no in His teaching never once broke a word. His silence before Pilate, Matthew 27:12-14, shows a man whose speech was never hasty and whose trust was in the Father. The one who has kept every vow is the only one who can sustain the sinner who has not.

It would be forced to find a Christ in every detail, such as the dream or the messenger. The point is that a book about the limits of human effort puts, at its center, a call to reverence that only a Mediator can make possible.
study.god:
The central statement is verse 2: God is in heaven and you are on earth. It is the book's clearest declaration of divine transcendence. It does not say God is far away or indifferent, for the whole passage presupposes that He hears vows and will be angry at a broken one, verse 6. It says He is other. Solomon's prayer asks whether God will really dwell on earth, since even the highest heaven cannot contain Him, 1 Kings 8:27, and the psalmist says the highest heavens belong to the LORD, Psalm 115:16. The Teacher draws the practical conclusion that a creature should not talk to the Creator as an equal.

The passage shows a God who listens and judges words. He hears what is said in His house, and He takes no pleasure in fools, verse 4. Verse 6 asks why He should be angry at your words and destroy the work of your hands, which suggests that careless speech has real consequences. Jesus says the same: people will give an account for every careless word, Matthew 12:36-37. The God of the temple is not a distant idea but the one who hears.

It shows God as one who desires truth in the heart. In Samuel's words, obedience is better than sacrifice, 1 Samuel 15:22; in Isaiah, God esteems the one who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at His word, Isaiah 66:2. This does not make God hard to please. Psalm 25:14 says the LORD confides in those who fear Him, and Psalm 5:7 shows the worshiper entering by God's loving devotion and bowing in reverence. The fear He asks for is the fear of someone who knows who He is, and it is the gateway to His friendship.

The passage shows how God holds together nearness and majesty. The same book that calls Him a God in heaven says He gives bread, work and joy from His hand, 2:24. A believer does not have to choose between a God who is too great to approach and a God who is too small to fear. Hebrews 12:28-29 puts both in one sentence: we receive an unshakable kingdom, we offer worship with reverence and awe, and our God is a consuming fire.

For worship, the passage asks for silence before speech, listening before offering, and honesty before promises. Habakkuk 2:20 says, 'the LORD is in His holy temple; let all the earth be silent before Him,' and Psalm 46:10 says, 'Be still and know that I am God.' The instruction is a call to let God be God.

crossReferences.note: The Law says not to be slow to keep a vow, that refusing to vow is no sin, and to follow through on what comes from your lips. The Teacher's verses 4 and 5 are close to a sermon on this text, and the Hebrew phrase for 'do not delay' is shared.

Samuel tells Saul that obedience is better than sacrifice and attentiveness better than the fat of rams. It stands behind the Teacher's preference for listening over the sacrifice of fools, and shows that the concern is old.

A person who swears thoughtlessly is guilty when he realizes it and must confess and bring an offering. The provision explains the temptation of verse 6 to call a vow a mistake, and shows that God provides a way of confession, not excuse.

Jephthah's vow before battle committed him to offer whatever came out of his house, and the cost fell on his daughter. It is the sharpest biblical case of why a rash vow is dangerous and why the Teacher says it is better not to vow.

Hannah's vow to dedicate a son to the LORD is the model of a vow made in sincerity and kept. She fulfills it in 1 Samuel 1:24-28, and her story shows what the Teacher means by paying what you promise.

Solomon asks at the dedication whether God will really dwell on earth when the highest heaven cannot contain Him. It supplies the theology behind 'God is in heaven and you are on earth,' and warns that the temple itself must never domesticate God.
Where words are many, sin is unavoidable, and the one who restrains his lips is wise. The proverb is a general rule for speech, while the Teacher applies it to speech before God.
The psalmist prays, 'Set a guard, O LORD, over my mouth.' The Teacher gives the instruction and the psalmist turns it into a prayer, admitting that the discipline of speech needs God's help.

Jesus tells His followers to let their yes be yes and their no be no instead of swearing oaths. It carries the Teacher's concern for honest promises to its simplest form: the speaker's word should be reliable on its own.

Jesus warns against babbling like pagans who think many words will be heard, since the Father knows what we need. It is verse 2's teaching on few words, with a gospel reason: the God who hears is a Father.

Believers can draw near through the blood of Jesus and the curtain of His body, with a sincere heart and full assurance. It fulfills the opening instruction to draw near, by showing how a sinner can come into God's house at all.

Because we receive an unshakable kingdom, we worship with reverence and awe, for our God is a consuming fire. It carries the fear of verse 7 into the new covenant and shows that grace does not remove awe.

study.oneStory:
From the garden onward, the Bible's story is about whether human beings will walk with God in His presence. In Eden the man and woman heard the sound of the LORD God walking in the garden. After the fall they hid, and cherubim guarded the way back, Genesis 3:8, 3:24. Everything that follows is a story of a God who makes a way to be near and a people who keep needing to be taught how to come. The tabernacle and the temple were God's answer, and the rules for sacrifice, priests and vows were the guardrails.

Ecclesiastes 5 sits in that story at a sobering moment. Israel has the temple, and the Teacher watches people enter it carelessly, with rituals and promises that do not rest on a listening heart. The prophets will say the same more sharply, in Isaiah 29:13 and Hosea 6:6. The passage answers a question left open since Eden: what does it look like to come before a holy God? It looks like reverence, attention and truth.

It also sets up a longing. If the way in requires a listening heart and perfect promises, who can come? The book itself does not say. It ends with the command to fear God and keep His commandments, and the reader is left wanting someone who has done it. The prophets look for a servant whose ears are opened, and Psalm 40 sketches him.

He comes in Jesus. He is the house, the priest, the offering and the perfect worshiper. John 1:14 says the Word 'made His dwelling among us,' and the tearing of the veil shows the way open. Believers are made a spiritual house and a holy priesthood, 1 Peter 2:5, and are taught still to worship with reverence and awe.

The story ends in a city where no temple is needed because 'the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple,' as Revelation 21:22 puts it. There the curse is gone, the servants worship, and they see His face, Revelation 22:3-4. The careful steps, the few words and the kept vows of Ecclesiastes 5 are the training of the heart for that day. Until then, believers come to God as the Teacher asks: listening first, speaking little, promising honestly, and standing in awe.

quiz.q: What posture does the Teacher urge for coming to the house of God, 5:1?

options.text: Guarded steps and a readiness to listen, rather than the empty offering of fools.
options.note: Worship begins with reverence and a listening heart, not careless talk.

options.text: A humble and attentive approach to God.
options.note: True, though the verse specifically contrasts listening with the sacrifice of fools.

options.text: Bringing the most impressive sacrifice you can afford.
options.note: The verse values a listening heart over the mere act of sacrifice.

options.text: Approaching God however feels natural in the moment.
options.note: The whole point is to guard your steps rather than come casually.

quiz.q: Why does the Teacher say to let your words be few, 5:2?

options.text: Because God is in heaven and you are on earth, a gap that calls for reverence.
options.note: The Creator creature distance is the reason for restraint before God.

options.text: Because we should be humble and thoughtful when we speak to God.
options.note: True, and the verse grounds this in God being in heaven while we are on earth.

options.text: Because God does not want to hear from us very often.
options.note: God invites us to draw near; the point is reverence, not distance.

options.text: Because prayer does not really matter to God.
options.note: The passage assumes real worship; it warns against careless words, not against prayer.

quiz.q: What does the Teacher teach about vows in 5:4-6?

options.text: Keep them without delay; better not to vow than to make a vow and break it.
options.note: Faithfulness to what we promise God is the heart of these verses.

options.text: Be careful about the promises you make to God.
options.note: True, but the specific command is to fulfill the vow rather than excuse it away.

options.text: Vows to God can be undone by explaining they were a mistake.
options.note: Verse 6 warns against exactly this, calling the mouth's words to account.

options.text: It does not matter whether you keep a vow or not.
options.note: The passage treats vows with great seriousness before God.

quiz.q: What single command does the passage land on in 5:7?

options.text: Fear God, the anchor set against the vapor of many words and dreams.
options.note: Fear God is the summit here and becomes the book's conclusion.

options.text: Avoid speaking too much, since many words are empty.
options.note: True to the verse's first half, but its climax is the command to fear God.

options.text: Pay attention to your dreams as messages from God.
options.note: The verse treats many dreams as vapor, not as revelation to heed.

options.text: Make as many vows as you can to please God.
options.note: The passage counsels caution with vows, not multiplying them.

quiz.q: What does fear God mean in this passage?

options.text: Covenant reverence, the awed and trusting respect of the creature for the Creator.
options.note: The fear of God is the beginning of wisdom, not cringing dread.

options.text: A serious, respectful caution in how we approach God.
options.note: Close, though biblical fear is fuller, a worshiping reverence, not mere caution.

options.text: Being afraid that God is waiting to punish us.
options.note: The fear commanded is reverent awe, which in Christ becomes the love of children.

options.text: A vague feeling of religious guilt.
options.note: Fear of God is a settled, worshiping reverence, not free floating guilt.

questions: The Teacher says to draw near to listen rather than to rush into speech. When you come to God, are you mostly talking or mostly listening, and what might change if you listened more?
God is in heaven and you are on earth. How would a fresh sense of that distance reshape the way you pray and worship this week?
He warns against vows made lightly and broken easily. Is there a promise you have made to God that you have quietly let slide, and what would faithfulness look like now?
Many words, like many dreams, can be vapor. Where has your religious talk outrun your actual listening and obedience?
Fear God is the anchor the whole book reaches for. What would it mean for reverent awe of God to steady you in a season where so much else feels fleeting?

translationNotes.note: Futility translates hevel, literally vapor or breath, the book's keyword; the fool's many words, like a tangle of dreams, are as empty and fleeting as breath.
God here, as throughout Ecclesiastes, is Elohim, the sovereign Creator; the phrase in 5:2, God is in heaven and you are on earth, sets the tone of reverence for the whole passage.
The messenger can also be rendered angel, as the footnote of the source notes; either way the point is that excusing a broken vow to God's representative does not undo the offense.
